{
  "text": "## The Efficacy of Postoperative Prophylactic Antibiotics in Orthognathic Surgery: A Prospective Study in Le Fort I Osteotomy and Bilateral Intraoral Vertical Ramus Osteotomy\n\n## INTRODUCTION\nAntibiotics are used to treat and prevent postoperative infections. In 1960, it was reported that pathogens are present during surgery[1],[2] regardless of how aseptic the surgery might appear. Moreover, the correlation between prophylactic antibiotics and postoperative wound infections was demonstrated. Therefore, prophylactic antibiotics are now used in almost all surgical procedures. The most effective method of antibiotic prophylaxis is the preoperative administration of antibiotics because it can act at the time when the wound is potentially contaminated by bacteria.[2]\u207b[4] On the other hand, it was also reported that the use of antibiotics after 3 - 4 hours of a bacterial invasion is unsuitable.[5]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics are generally administered both preoperatively and postoperatively. Hence, the effects of the indiscriminate method and period of administration are unclear, considering the multiple factors that contribute to postoperative wound infections.[6]\u207b[8]\n\nThe use of antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial even in orthognathic surgery, which is a representative procedure for oral and maxillofacial surgery. There are reports show no increase in the incidence of infection without the administration of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics.[9],[10] On the other hand, there are reports to suggest the necessity of continuous antibiotic administration.[11] However, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without a specific medical history. Moreover, the number of factors associated with the development of postoperative wound infections decreases as the procedure becomes more generalized and its technique advances.\n\nThe aims of this clinical study were to evaluate the prevalence of postoperative wound infections with or without antibiotic prophylaxis after orthognathic surgery in young patients without any specific medical history, and to identify criteria for appropriate use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery.\n\n## PATIENTS AND METHODS\nFifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history, and who were to undergo orthognathic surgical procedures at the department of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the dental hospital of Yonsei University were enrolled in this study. A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon with the aid of trained nurses and residents under hypotensive general anesthesia. No bone grafts were performed. The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours. During surgery, maxillomandibular fixation was placed using steel wires, and drainage tubes were placed on both sides of the mandible. The drainage tubes were removed 2 days after surgery. The wires used for maxillomandibular fixation were removed and the sutures were taken out from the wounds 7 days after surgery. The patients received a non-steroid anti-inflammatory drug (Ketorolac trometamine 30 mg) intramuscularly immediately after surgery and every 6 hours until the next day. Compression bandages and ice packs were applied to the facial area until the second day after surgery.\n\nThe 56 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel: an experimental and control group. The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo. The control group also received 1.0 g of Cefpiramide 30 minutes before surgery as well as twice daily until 3 days after surgery. The patients were evaluated every day during the first 3 days and at the end of the 1st and 2nd week after surgery for any postoperative infections in reference to the criteria for defining a surgical site infection (SSI), recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).[12] Postoperative wound infection was defined by at least 1 of the following criteria:\n\nStatistical analysis was performed using a \u03c7\u00b2-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the College of Dentistry, Yonsei University (YUDC).\n\n## RESULTS\nThe mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84) with male-female ratio of 4 : 3. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 40 minutes. The mean (SD) age of the control group was 24.3 years (6.33) with male-female ratio of 1 : 1. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 55 minutes.\n\nThere were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group, observed 2 weeks after surgery (Table 1). One patient in the experimental group was diagnosed with an infection by facial swelling, redness and sinus haziness in the waters' view, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with a postoperative infection by swelling and redness, and pain on the mandibular area. Therefore, the wounds were opened by a surgeon and the patients were treated with antibiotics. However, only 1 patient in the control group developed wound dehiscence only without any drainage, fever, or swelling in the maxillary area. According to the \u03c7\u00b2-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).\n\n[Table 1: Results according to the Postoperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis \u2014 image only, no cells; see tables]\n\n## DISCUSSION\nThe method of antibiotic prophylaxis is determined by an evaluation of the patient, procedure, and surgical wound. The preoperative and immediate postoperative administration of antibiotics is a method generally used for antibiotic prophylaxis in almost all surgical procedures. However, antibiotics are continuously used postoperatively in most procedures because it is difficult to assess the factors associated with postoperative wound infections or appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis method.\n\nOn the other hand, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without an underlying illness or comorbidity. Moreover, the number of factors affecting the development of postoperative wound infections decreases with the improvement of the surgical instruments, materials, techniques, and more generalized procedure.\n\nPeterson[13] suggested that the prophylactic antibiotic administration for postoperative wound infections in oral and maxillofacial surgery should be performed if there is a strong probability of infection, and appropriate antibiotics must be given in high-dose but for only a short period of time. Orthognathic surgeries are classified as clean contaminated procedures with postoperative wound infection of 10% to 15%, and Peterson[13] reported that an incidence of an anticipated infection in oral clean contaminated surgery could be reduced by using prophylactic antibiotics. Zijderveld et al.[14] suggested that the incidence of postoperative infections (52.6%) increased without the administration of prophylactic antibiotics. Martis and Karabouta[9] suggested that the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery is unnecessary, and Lindeboom et al.[15] also suggested that the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics (clindamycin) is unnecessary in orthognathic surgery (SSRO). Furthermore, Fridrich et al.[16] and Baqain et al.[17] suggested that the long-term use of antibiotics does not decrease the frequency of postoperative infections. However, wide range of patient's age, small group size, and various osteomies may cause difficulties when precisely evaluating the efficacy of prophylactic antibiotics.\n\nTherefore, this study was undertaken to examine the prevalence of postoperative wound infections in young patients after orthognathic surgery (Le Fort I osteotomy and bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy) with or without the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics. Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of \u03b1= 0.05 and a test power \u03b2= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.[17] In this study, wound infections were observed in both groups, however, the number was small. This was attributed to the followings: the patients were young without a specific medical history, patients had no preoperative wound infections, no bone graft had been performed during surgery, the surgical procedures such as IVRO were less traumatic with a short duration, the tissue trauma during surgery was minimal due to the systematization of orthognathic surgery and the improvement of techniques, and wound control such as postoperative blood or exudate was properly performed.\n\nThe types of antibiotics used are important factors to consider for prophylactic antibiotic treatment. Penicillin is the representative antibiotic used as a prophylaxis during intraoral surgery and for the primary treatment of dental infections. Spaey et al[18] suggested the use of amoxicillin-clavulanate along with drain usage during SSRO in a study of antibiotic administration. In this study, third-generation cephalosporin antibiotics were administered before surgery, which is believed to be a possible prophylactic antibiotic that may be used in orthognathic surgery because most bacteria cultured during a dental infection are susceptible to third-generation cephalosporin.[19] There has been an increase in infections due to anaerobic and Gram-negative organisms,[20] and most wound infections after orthognathic surgery are caused by Gram negative bacteria.[21]\n\nIf a post-operative wound infection occurs despite the effective prophylactic antibiotic administration before surgery, it could be concluded that the bacteria in the infected wound are not sensitive to the prophylactic antibiotics administered, and in such cases, an appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be determined by a culture test of the bacteria found in the infected region.[21],[22]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics reduce the risk of postoperative wound infections, which leads to a lower number of hospitalization days, reduced cost, and improved social life. However, the long-term use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics may lead to several problems, such as various allergic reactions, increased cost, changes in resident bacterial colony in vivo, or appearance of resistant bacteria.[7],[23]\n\nMore studies with much larger numbers of patients are needed on the administration of prophylactic antibiotics during orthognathic surgery and other oral and maxillofacial procedures. In addition, further research on properly appropriated use of antibiotic prophylaxis is warranted in order to minimize the use of prophylactic antibiotics and their adverse effects and problems. In the present study, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who did not. Therefore, prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections.",

headline.statement: Both baseline age standard deviations in Table 1 are larger than any sample of 28 patients aged "in their 20s" could possibly produce, so the age row and the paper's own description of who was enrolled cannot both be correct.
headline.evidence: Methods: "Fifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history ... were enrolled in this study." Table 1: "Age (Mean±SD) 23.9±5.84 yrs [experimental, n=28] / 24.3±6.33 yrs [control, n=28]", repeated verbatim in Results: "The mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84) ... the control group was 24.3 years (6.33)". For n = 28 confined to [20, 30] -- the most generous possible reading of "in their 20s" -- the largest attainable sample SD is 5.0918. Reported SDs are 5.84 (115% of the ceiling) and 6.33 (124%). Under the strict [20, 29] reading the ceiling is 4.5826 and the reported values reach 127% and 138% of it.
headline.plain: The paper says every patient was in their twenties, but the spread it reports for patients' ages is wider than is arithmetically possible for a group of 28 people all aged between 20 and 30. One of those two statements has to be wrong. This affects how the study describes its patients -- and the argument that its narrow age range makes it better than earlier studies -- but not its main infection result, which checks out.

findings.computed: For n = 28 on [20, 30], max attainable sample SD = 5.0918; reported 5.84 is 114.7% of it and 6.33 is 124.3% of it (both `impossible`). On the strict [20, 29] reading the ceiling is 4.5826 and the values reach 127.4% and 138.1%. SD/SE confusion is ruled out: read as a standard error, 6.33 implies an SD of 33.5 years, 6.6 times the ceiling, and the tool returns likely_interpretation = "neither". Bracketing the minimum age span that would admit SD = 6.33: a 12-year span (20-32) still fails (SD is 103.6% of the ceiling); 13 years (20-33) is the first that succeeds, and even there the SD sits at 95.6% of the theoretical maximum, attainable only if patients are stacked almost entirely at the two extremes.
findings.assumptions: The numeric bound [20, 30) is my mapping of the paper's English phrase "in their 20s"; the paper gives no explicit numeric inclusion range. The mapping is forced by the language, and the finding is deliberately reported against the generous [20, 30] reading rather than the strict [20, 29] one so that it does not turn on how tightly the phrase is read. Table 1 is an image in the JATS XML and pdfplumber returned no table grid, so the eight cells were read from PDF page 3; the two age cells are independently corroborated by the machine-extracted Results prose, which prints the identical means and SDs. Both arms fail separately, so this is not a single mistyped cell.
findings.plain: To say the average age was 24 with a spread of 6.3 years is to say a fair number of patients were in their thirties and a fair number in their teens. But the paper states everyone enrolled was in their twenties, and no group of 28 people all aged 20 to 30 can have a spread that wide -- the arithmetic simply does not allow it. The same problem appears in both treatment groups, so it is not one mistyped number. Reconciling the reported spread would need patients ranging over at least 13 years, mostly clustered at the two extremes. This matters twice over: the description of who was studied is wrong somewhere, and the paper argues in its discussion that its narrow age range is what makes it more reliable than earlier work. It does not, however, affect the infection comparison that is the study's main result.

consequence.explanation: Undermines the Table 1 description of the enrolled sample and the Discussion's claim that a narrow patient age range distinguishes this study from prior work criticised for "wide range of patient's age"; the primary infection comparison does not use these values and is unaffected.

findings.title: Negative conclusion drawn from five total events, with no interval and a design powered only for a 30-percentage-point difference
findings.location: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, paragraph beginning "Therefore, this study was undertaken"; Discussion, final paragraph
findings.reported: "Conclusion: Prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections." Sample size justification: "The samples were selected at a significance level of α=0.05 and a test power β=0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%." No confidence interval, odds ratio, risk difference or test statistic is reported anywhere in the paper.
findings.computed: The trial was sized to detect 5% versus 35%, a 30-percentage-point gap. The observed contrast was 3 of 28 (10.7%) versus 2 of 28 (7.1%). The recalculation recovers a Fisher odds ratio of 1.56, i.e. the point estimate favours the arm that did receive postoperative antibiotics, on a total of five events. The paper also mislabels its own parameter: β is the Type II error rate, so β = 0.20 corresponds to power = 0.80, not to "a test power β=0.20".
findings.assumptions: No arithmetic here is impossible; the concern is inferential and the severity is asserted, not computed. absence_of_evidence could not be run because the paper reports no interval for any effect measure, and verify_power_analysis could not be run because it requires Cohen's h, which the paper does not state and which I am barred from computing by hand. The odds ratio of 1.56 is taken from the chi-squared recalculation, not computed independently.
findings.plain: The study concludes that continuing antibiotics after surgery may be unnecessary. But it was designed only to detect a very large difference -- 5% of patients infected in one group versus 35% in the other -- and it saw nothing of the sort: three infections against two. A trial built to spot a gap that big cannot tell you that a smaller but still clinically important gap is absent. The paper also reports no range of plausible values around its result, so a reader has no way to judge how large a real difference could still be hiding in these numbers. Notably, the point estimate that can be recovered actually leans slightly toward the patients who kept taking antibiotics doing better, on a total of five infections across the whole study. The finding here is not that the conclusion is wrong, but that the study is too small to establish it.

consequence.explanation: The Abstract's and Discussion's conclusion that prolonged prophylaxis "may not be necessary" is an absence-of-evidence inference from five events, with no interval reported to bound the effect the trial could have missed.

findings.title: Chi-squared test applied to a table whose expected counts fall to 2.5, with no assumption check and no exact alternative
findings.location: Results, final paragraph (repeated in Abstract); Patients and Methods, statistical analysis sentence
findings.reported: "Statistical analysis was performed using a χ²-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0)." "According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections ... (p = 0.639)." No χ² statistic, no degrees of freedom, and no assumption check are reported; Fisher's exact test is not mentioned.
findings.computed: An uncorrected Pearson chi-squared on [[3,25],[2,26]] gives χ² = 0.2196, df = 1, p = 0.6393, matching the reported 0.639 exactly, so the test the authors ran is identifiable and its arithmetic is correct. However both infection cells have an expected count of 2.5, below the conventional minimum of 5 for an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared. Fisher's exact test on the same table returns p = 1.00.
findings.assumptions: The expected-count threshold of 5 is the conventional rule of thumb, not a mathematical bound; the paper states no assumption check either way. The cell counts 3/28 and 2/28 are taken from Table 1 and are independently confirmed by the Results narrative, whose breakdown of infected patients (one plus "the other 4") sums to five.
findings.plain: The single statistical test in this paper is the standard chi-squared test, and the number it produces is arithmetically correct. But that test is not valid on a table this sparse: with only five infections spread across 56 patients, the counts are far too small for the approximation the test relies on. The appropriate test for such small numbers, Fisher's exact test, gives a p-value of 1.00 rather than 0.639. This does not reverse the conclusion -- neither test finds a difference -- but the reported 0.639 makes the comparison look more precise than it is, and the paper neither checks the assumption nor mentions the exact alternative.

consequence.explanation: The headline p = 0.639 comes from a test whose assumptions this table violates; the appropriate exact test gives p = 1.00, so the "no significant difference" conclusion holds but the reported precision does not.

findings.title: Baseline balance not assessable from two rows, one of which rests on the impossible age SDs
findings.reported: Age 23.9±5.84 vs 24.3±6.33 (n = 28 each); Sex (Male : Female) 16 : 12 vs 14 : 14. The paper reports no baseline p-values and makes no explicit claim of baseline balance.
findings.computed: The dispersion tool returns τ̂ = 2.40 (90% CI 1.87 to 4.09), nominally indicating under-dispersion, from derived baseline p-values of 0.81 (age) and 0.59 (sex). I do not treat this as a finding. The estimate rests on n_rows = 2, the correlation-aware CSF cross-check on the same p-values returned `indeterminate`, and the K-S test against uniformity gives p = 0.33. Decisively, the age p-value of 0.81 is derived from the very SDs shown above to exceed their mathematical ceiling, and inflating an SD mechanically pushes that p-value upward -- so the apparent uniformity is partly manufactured by an input already known to be corrupt.
findings.assumptions: The tool was run with design = parallel_rct as stated by the paper ("randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel"). Downgraded from the sweep's `suspicious` to `indeterminate` for the reasons above. This must NOT be read in the opposite direction either: 0.81 and 0.59 are not the Carlisle signature of near-unity baseline p-values, and nothing here provides reassurance that the allocation was sound -- there is simply too little baseline data to judge.
findings.plain: A standard check asks whether the two groups look suspiciously similar at the start, which can be a sign that patients were not really assigned at random. Here that check cannot be done: the paper reports only two baseline characteristics, age and sex, and the age figures are the ones already shown to be impossible. Two characteristics is far too few to draw any conclusion from, and one of them is unreliable. This is a gap in what can be verified, not evidence that anything is wrong -- but neither should it be read as confirmation that the randomisation worked.

consequence.explanation: No claim in the paper depends on this; it records that the randomisation cannot be independently audited from the baseline data reported.

findings.title: Unblinded trial with the primary outcome adjudicated by the operating surgeon
findings.location: Patients and Methods, paragraphs 1-2 and the CDC criteria list
findings.reported: "The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo." "A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon." The adopted CDC criteria include "pain or tenderness, localized swelling, redness or heat" and, as criterion 4, "Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon or attending physician."
findings.computed: No tool in the suite evaluates blinding; this is a reading of the Methods, recorded so it is not silently omitted. Allocation itself was by Excel-generated randomisation codes, which is a defensible method, so the concern is outcome assessment rather than allocation.
findings.assumptions: This is a qualitative risk-of-bias judgement with no numeric content, asserted rather than computed. It implies no direction of error.
findings.reproduction: No runnable command: no forensic tool in this suite evaluates blinding or outcome-assessment bias. This finding is a direct reading of the Methods text quoted above.
findings.plain: Patients in the no-antibiotic group were not given a dummy treatment, so everyone involved knew who was getting what. Two of the four criteria used to declare an infection are judgement calls -- swelling, redness, pain -- and one of them is simply the surgeon deciding an infection is present. Since a single surgeon operated on every patient and was not kept unaware of group assignment, the counts of three infections versus two carry less weight than they would in a blinded study. This does not mean the counts are wrong, only that they rest on unblinded judgement.

consequence.explanation: Weakens the evidential value of the 3-versus-2 event counts underlying the primary comparison, without implying a direction of error.

findings.title: No participant flow, attrition figures, or trial registration reported
findings.location: Patients and Methods, paragraph 1; Results throughout
findings.reported: "Fifty-six patients in their 20s ... were enrolled in this study." All 56 appear in the analysis (28 per arm in Table 1). No exclusions, withdrawals or losses to follow-up are mentioned anywhere, there is no CONSORT flow diagram, and no trial registration number appears. IRB approval by Yonsei University College of Dentistry is stated.
findings.computed: No tool applies: the finding is the absence of numbers rather than a value to test. The group sizes 28/28/56 are not suspiciously round in the 50/100 sense, so no round-N concern arises, and all reported counts reconcile exactly.
findings.assumptions: Complete retention is not implausible over a two-week postoperative window in a hospitalised surgical cohort, and prospective registration was not yet routine for a 2009 paper accepted in April 2008. Recorded as a transparency gap of its era, not as a signal in itself.
findings.reproduction: No runnable command: this records the absence of reported figures, and no forensic tool takes "not reported" as an input.
findings.plain: The paper never says whether any patient dropped out, was excluded, or missed follow-up -- all 56 enrolled patients simply appear in the results. Over a two-week window after surgery that is quite believable, so this is not suspicious on its own. It does mean a reader cannot independently check the analysed group against the group originally enrolled.

consequence.explanation: The analysed sample cannot be reconciled against enrolment independently, though every reported count is internally consistent.

not_checked.reason: The JATS XML reports Table 1 as image_only with n_rows: 0 -- it is a picture and carries no cells. pdfplumber also returned no tables, rejecting all five page candidates as segmented prose. The eight cell values were therefore read from PDF page 3 text rather than machine-extracted from a grid. The two age cells and the four counts are independently corroborated by the Results prose, which the XML did render as machine-readable text and which prints the same means, SDs, sex ratios and infection counts.

verify_power_analysis was not run. For two proportions it requires Cohen's h; the paper states raw proportions (5% and 35%) and converting them needs an arcsine transform. Computing that by hand is barred, and supplying a self-computed effect size would make the tool's verdict unauditable. The substantive design point is reported instead, and requires no arithmetic.

not_checked.location: Abstract Conclusion and Discussion, final paragraph
not_checked.reason: absence_of_evidence was not run. It requires ci_low and ci_high, and the paper reports no confidence interval for any effect measure -- not for the risk difference, not for an odds ratio. Deriving an interval by hand is barred.

GRIM and SPRITE were not run. Both require integer-valued observations, and the paper nowhere states that ages were recorded as whole years. Forcing data_type='integer' to obtain a verdict would rest the result on an assumption the paper never makes. The sweep's refusal here was correct and I did not override it.

debit_check was not run. DEBIT requires a binary variable reported as a mean with an SD; sex is printed as a male:female count ratio (16:12, 14:14), with no mean or SD, so the check has no applicable inputs.

multiplicity_report was not run, deliberately. The paper contains exactly one inferential test of one hypothesis; running a multiplicity analysis on a family of one would manufacture the appearance of a problem that does not exist.

grimu_check and grimu_coexistence were not run. Rank-sum granularity applies only to Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon p-values; this paper's only p-value comes from a chi-squared test, and applying GRIM-U to it would be the most likely route to a false accusation.

The average duration of surgery is reported as "3 hours and 40 minutes" and "3 hours and 55 minutes" with no dispersion, no n-specific figures and no test, so no granularity or consistency check applies. The only stated bound, "The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours", is satisfied by both values.
No supplementary files accompany this paper in the provided directory; only the XML and the PDF are present. Recorded as genuinely absent rather than present-but-unreadable.

statcheck recovered zero statistics, not through tool failure but because the paper never prints a test statistic or degrees of freedom anywhere, giving only a bare "p = 0.639". There is no APA-form triple to audit; verification was possible only because the underlying cell counts appear in Table 1.

limitations: This agent reads text and tables only. It does not see figures, and no claim in this report rests on anything read off an image. This paper contains no figures.

Table 1 is an image in the publisher XML and pdfplumber recovered no table grid from the PDF, so its eight cells were read from PDF page 3 text rather than machine-extracted. The two age values that carry the headline finding are independently corroborated by the machine-extracted Results prose, which prints identical means and SDs; the count cells are corroborated by the Results narrative and by the chi-squared recalculation. Confidence in these specific values is therefore high despite the extraction route.

The numeric age bound [20, 30) is my mapping of the paper's phrase "in their 20s", which the paper never states as an explicit numeric inclusion criterion. The finding is reported against this generous reading rather than the strict [20, 29] one precisely so that it does not turn on how tightly the phrase is read.

The paper's sample-size calculation could not be reproduced: verify_power_analysis requires Cohen's h and the paper reports only raw proportions. The design criticism made here rests on the stated proportions themselves, not on a recomputed power figure.

No confidence interval could be computed for the infection comparison, because the paper reports none and deriving one by hand is barred. The statement that the data cannot bound the effect being missed is therefore qualitative.
Baseline balance could not be meaningfully assessed: the paper reports only two baseline characteristics, and one of them is the age row already shown to be arithmetically impossible.

The specific thing this review could not resolve: whether the two age standard deviations are transcription or typesetting errors, or whether the enrolled sample was not in fact confined to patients in their twenties. Only the raw ages would settle it, and the distinction matters for how much of Table 1 a reader should rely on.

tables_checked: Table 1: Results according to the Postoperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis (image_only in the JATS XML; grid read from PDF page 3 and cross-confirmed against the Results prose; 8 data cells, all covered by targeted tools, 0 of 8 by the batched check_table pass)

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1 and the Results text both give the mean age as 23.9 ± 5.84 years (experimental, n = 28) and 24.3 ± 6.33 years (control, n = 28), while the Methods state that enrolment was limited to "Fifty-six patients in their 20s". For 28 patients aged between 20 and 30 the largest attainable standard deviation is 5.09. Could you provide the observed minimum and maximum age in each arm, so the reported dispersion can be reconciled with the stated enrolment criterion?
questions_for_authors.why: This is the only question that can settle whether the headline finding is a transcription/typesetting error confined to two cells or a misdescription of the enrolled sample, which in turn determines whether the Discussion's narrow-age-range argument stands.

questions_for_authors.question: The primary comparison is 3 of 28 versus 2 of 28, which gives expected counts of 2.5 in both infection cells. Was Fisher's exact test considered as an alternative to the reported χ²-test, and could you report the χ² statistic and degrees of freedom alongside the p = 0.639?
questions_for_authors.why: Establishes whether the assumption violation was noticed and how the analysis was specified; Fisher's exact on the same table gives p = 1.00, and the paper reports no test statistic or df that would let a reader identify the test independently.

questions_for_authors.question: The Discussion states that "The samples were selected at a significance level of α=0.05 and a test power β=0.20", with a smaller infection rate of 5% and an estimated difference of 30%. Could you confirm that β = 0.20 denotes 80% power, and provide the calculation showing that n = 28 per group achieves that power for 5% versus 35%?
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves the parameter-labelling ambiguity and lets the sample-size justification be reproduced; it also documents the effect size the trial was actually designed to detect, against an observed contrast of 10.7% versus 7.1%.

questions_for_authors.question: Given that the experimental group "did not receive the placebo" and that CDC criterion 4 is "Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon or attending physician", who assessed each patient for surgical site infection, and was that assessor aware of the treatment allocation?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines the risk of bias in the primary outcome; with a single operating surgeon, an unblinded design and partly subjective criteria, the answer bears directly on how much weight the 3-versus-2 event counts can carry.

questions_for_authors.question: Were any of the 56 enrolled patients excluded, withdrawn, or lost to follow-up before the two-week assessment, and was this trial registered before enrolment began?
questions_for_authors.why: The paper reports no participant flow and no registration number, so the analysed sample cannot be reconciled against enrolment; a simple statement would close the gap.

input.report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is a 56-patient prospective trial from Yonsei University comparing a single preoperative dose of cefpiramide against the same dose continued twice daily for three postoperative days, in patients undergoing Le Fort I osteotomy with bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy. Allocation was by Excel-generated randomisation codes, 28 per arm. The primary outcome was surgical site infection at two weeks, judged against CDC criteria. Three infections occurred in the arm receiving no postoperative antibiotics and two in the arm that continued them; the authors report a chi-squared p of 0.639 and conclude that prolonged prophylaxis "may not be necessary".

## What verifies, and it is worth saying first

The count layer of this paper is clean. Every sum reconciles exactly with zero tolerance: 16 + 12 and 14 + 14 both give 28, the arms sum to 56, the five infections split 3 and 2, and the narrative breakdown of infected patients -- one diagnosed by sinus haziness plus "the other 4" -- sums to the same five. The sex ratios quoted in prose, 4:3 and 1:1, match the table's 16:12 and 14:14. The single inferential statistic reproduces exactly: an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared on 3/28 versus 2/28 returns 0.2196 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.6393, against a reported 0.639. That recalculation also resolves an ambiguity in the Results narrative, pinning the tested counts to 3 versus 2 and confirming that the one patient with wound dehiscence was not folded into the infection count. And the observed infection rates, roughly 11% and 7%, sit close to the 10-15% the authors themselves cite for clean-contaminated orthognathic procedures, so nothing in the outcome data is implausible on its face.

Note what made that verification possible. The paper prints no chi-squared statistic and no degrees of freedom anywhere -- only a bare p. Independent checking worked solely because the cell counts appear in Table 1, which is the reason cell counts outrank stated p-values in the verification hierarchy.

## The reasoning behind the triage

Three of the sweep's calls needed correcting or consolidating, and the reasoning matters more than the outcome.

The six separate age findings are one defect, not six. They reduce to a single statement -- the reported age dispersion cannot be reconciled with the stated sample -- approached from four directions: the strict reading of the enrolment phrase, a deliberately generous reading, the SD-versus-SE rescue attempt, and a bracketing of the minimum age span that would work. All four agree, and reporting them as separate hits would inflate the apparent weight of one problem. They are merged.

The baseline-dispersion result required correcting in the opposite direction from usual. The tool returned a precision multiplier of 2.40, nominally under-dispersion, which the sweep graded `suspicious`. I have downgraded it to `indeterminate`, and the reason is specific rather than cautious: the estimate rests on two baseline rows, the correlation-aware cross-check on the same p-values returned `indeterminate`, and the age p-value of 0.81 is derived from the very standard deviations shown to exceed their mathematical ceiling. Inflating an SD mechanically pushes that p-value upward, so the apparent uniformity is in part an artefact of an input already known to be corrupt. It should not be read the other way either -- 0.81 and 0.59 are nothing like the near-unity signature that indicates non-random allocation, and nothing here reassures anyone that the randomisation was sound. There is simply too little baseline data to judge, and that is the honest answer.

Finally, the sweep declined to run GRIM on the age means, on the ground that the paper nowhere states ages were recorded in whole years. That refusal was correct and I did not override it. Had ages been integers, both means would fail -- but that conclusion would rest entirely on an assumption the authors never made, and the age anomaly is established without it, from the paper's own words.

## What the numbers cannot settle

Two things about this trial sit outside arithmetic. The study was sized to detect a difference between a 5% and a 35% infection rate -- thirty percentage points -- and observed 10.7% against 7.1%. A trial built to spot a gap that large is close to blind to anything smaller, and the recovered odds ratio of 1.56 actually points, weakly and on five events, toward the arm that kept taking antibiotics. With no interval reported for any effect measure, a reader has no way to bound what this study could have missed. That is the gap between "we found no difference" and "there is no difference", and the Conclusion crosses it.

The second is assessment. The experimental group explicitly "did not receive the placebo", one surgeon operated on every patient, and the fourth of the four adopted CDC criteria is diagnosis by that surgeon. Allocation was sound in method; adjudication was not blinded. Three-versus-two is a fragile margin to rest on unblinded judgement.

## Verdict

The primary result of this paper checks out, and its counts are coherent throughout. But its baseline table contains an arithmetic contradiction against the paper's own description of who was enrolled, in both arms; its one test is invalid for the sparse table it was run on; and its clinical conclusion is stronger than five events and no interval can support. I would not rely on Table 1 without the raw ages, and I would not change practice on this study's conclusion.
